entry.title: What I Wish I Knew Before Starting Computer Science in College
entry.summary:
What I Wish I Knew Before Starting Computer Science in College
Starting CS in college? Congrats—and brace yourself. You’re about to learn a lot of code, and even more about yourself. Here’s what I wish I knew when I started: You don’t need to memorize every language's syntax. Real developers Google stuff all the time. You’re here to learn how to learn. Anyone can write code. But being a developer means: Solving problems
Communicating ideas
Working on teams
Knowing how to debug and test
Writing code someone else can understand Seriously. Write the ugly stuff. Break things. That’s how you learn. Bad code teaches you more than blank files ever will. Most students treat debugging as punishment. But it’s actually one of your most important tools. Learn to debug well and you'll level up faster than anyone around you. Your IDE. Your terminal. Your debugger. Your version control system. These aren’t extra—they’re essentials. Mastering your tools will make your life so much easier. Languages change. Frameworks come and go. But things like loops, conditionals, data structures, and algorithms? They’re forever. Learn them deeply. Imposter syndrome is real. Everyone’s faking it a little. Find your people, ask questions, and remember—you’re not supposed to be perfect. You’re not just learning to write code. You’re learning how to think like a developer. And that’s a skill you’ll carry for life. You’ve got this. 👊 👉 Read more no-BS tech advice at mullins.io
